description: Not an ancestral spirit but a real political office: the amenokal (amenukal) is the supreme traditional chief of a Tuareg confederation, head of an 'ettebel' (drum) chiefship among groups such as the Kel Ahaggar, Kel Adagh and Kel Air. Succession passes among the kin of a deceased holder, and authority rests on prestige and consensus rather than force.

research_notes: Amenukal is confirmed as the title of the highest Tuareg traditional chiefs, head of an ettebel (drum) chiefship, elected from the kin of a deceased chief. The 'Ancestral Spirit of Leadership who judges the dead' framing in the input is fabricated; description corrected to the attested institution.

description: An artificial being of Estonian folklore, the kratt is assembled from hay, straw, old tools or wooden implements and animated by a pact with the Devil, sealed by three drops of blood. It works tirelessly, fetching grain and stealing from neighbors, and must always be given a task, or it turns on its maker. A leak in the roof or a drawn circle forces it to spill its loot.
source: Estonian folklore collections; Wikipedia (Kratt)
research_notes: Kratt is a genuine, well-documented Estonian belief. Description retained the input's accurate core (object construct, devil pact, blood drops, tireless labor) with template phrases removed.

description: A hostile forest spirit of Estonian tradition, the kulmking (linked to Estonian 'külm', cold) is a malevolent being of the woods, bogs and remote wilds, dreaded more than the neutral forest guardians of Estonian nature belief and associated with the unholy dead. It is said to waylay travelers who enter its territory.
source: Folklore databases and popular retellings; no dedicated academic monograph located
research_notes: Name and forest-spirit role attested in folklore references (e.g., Mythlok); etymology from Estonian 'külm' (cold) is consistent. No academic source located, so quality kept at fair and description stays within documented appearance.

description: The douen (dwen) is a spirit of Grenadian and wider Trinidadian folklore: the soul of a child who died unbaptized, appearing as a faceless child under a wide straw hat, with feet turned backwards. It lures living children into the forest by calling or asking for help, and its reversed footprints make it impossible to track.
source: Grenadian oral tradition; Wikipedia (Douen)
research_notes: Douen is attested across Grenada and Trinidad. Backward feet, faceless head under a broad hat, and luring of children are the documented core; description trims redundancy while keeping these details.

description: Erzulie Freda is the lwa of love, beauty, luxury and feminine charm in Haitian Vodou, portrayed as a light-skinned woman in pink, blue, white and gold finery, adorned with jewelry and surrounded by mirrors, lace and perfume. Syncretized with Our Lady of Sorrows, she is both radiant and melancholy, weeping for the world's suffering.
source: Haitian Vodou scholarship; Wikipedia (Erzulie)
research_notes: Erzulie Freda is a canonical, well-documented lwa. Description condensed the input's detailed but over-long portrait, keeping the documented colors, offerings, vanity and sorrow aspects within the length limit.

description: Maboya is the feared evil spirit of the Island Carib (Kalinago), attested since the 1765 Encyclopédie, where Le Romain records that the Caribs of the Antilles dreaded its malign will and carved small grotesque figurines of wood, clay or resin, placed in canoes and huts. The word also came to mean 'evil' generally, and the boyez priest ritually warded the spirit away.

research_notes: Maboya/Maboyo is attested in an excellent primary source: the 1765 Encyclopédie entry by Le Romain describes the Carib devil-spirit and its carved idols, and the boyez priest. The input's 'colossal sky serpent' image derives from a modern content farm (Mythlok) and is not in the historical record; description corrected accordingly.

description: The moko jumbie is a towering, stilt-walking ancestral spirit of the Caribbean, and Saint Vincent preserves the oldest written record of the tradition: William Young's 1791 account of 'Moco Jumbies' among the island's Black Caribs, who performed in costumes blending African motifs with women's petticoats and dresses.

research_notes: Attested, with the oldest written reference (William Young, 1791, St. Vincent) and later descriptions by Charles Day. Description retains the documented 1791 detail and the guardian-tall-tall function.

description: The ol' hige is the Jamaican vampire-hag: an elderly woman bound by a diabolical pact who, by night, sheds her skin, hides it in a mortar or under a tree, and flies as a ball of fire to suck the blood of sleeping victims, often infants.
source: Jamaican oral tradition; Caribbean soucouyant lore (Wikipedia)
research_notes: Attested as the Jamaican form of the skin-shedding vampire hag (soucouyant/loogaroo). Rice-counting and hidden-skin details are documented; description kept the essential protective lore within length.

description: Papa Bois, 'Father of the Wood' in French Creole, is the guardian of the forest in Saint Lucian and wider Caribbean lore: an old, muscular man with cloven hooves, horns and a beard of living leaves who warns animals with a cow's horn and punishes wasteful hunters, sometimes by shapeshifting into a deer to lead them astray.

research_notes: Papa Bois is attested across the Francophone Caribbean. The input text described Grenada (wife Mama Glo) despite the Saint Lucia slug; description rewritten island-neutral, keeping the documented horn, deer-shapeshifting and guardian role.

description: The Ankou is the death-messenger of Breton folklore, a skeletal or shrouded figure who rides or drives a cart, gathering the souls of the dying; the last person to die in a parish becomes the Ankou for the following year, and the creaking of his wheels is a mortal omen.
source: Wikipedia (Ankou); Breton folklore collections
research_notes: Ankou is well attested as a Breton death figure (Brittany, France); the Cornwall attribution in the input is questionable, and the 'forest-spirit' archetype is wrong. Description corrected to the attested Breton tradition with the geographic note.

description: The bean sí (banshee) is the female death-spirit of Irish tradition whose wailing, keening cry foretells a death in the family; her name means 'woman of the fairy mounds' (sídhe). Long-haired and often seen combing her hair, she is attached to particular old families.
source: Wikipedia (Banshee); Irish folklore scholarship
research_notes: Bean Sídhe (banshee) is well attested in Irish tradition. The input content was entirely about the Scottish bean-nighe despite the Irish slug; description rewritten for the Irish banshee and the mismatch noted.

description: Goreu fab Custennin is not a shapeshifting spirit but a hero of the Welsh tale Culhwch ac Olwen in the Mabinogion: son of Custennin the giant and cousin to Arthur, he joins Culhwch's quest and, at the story's end, beheads the giant chieftain Ysbaddaden, whose fortress and lands he receives. research_notes: Goreu fab Custennin is attested as a human hero of Culhwch ac Olwen (kills Ysbaddaden, Arthur's cousin). The input's 'shapeshifting trickster spirit' is entirely fabricated; description corrected to the Mabinogion role.

description: Kalunga-ngombe is the Kimbundu god of the underworld in Angola, ruler of Kalunga, the sea and realm of the dead. description: The Kishi is a two-faced demon of Angolan (Kimbundu/Ambundu) folklore: from the front a handsome young man, from behind the head of a hyena with sharp teeth. He lures young women with charm and courtship, then turns and devours them.

description: Khazyr (Khyzyr) is the Turkmen form of al-Khidr, the immortal green prophet-guide of Islamic tradition, honored across Central Asia as a protector of travelers, wayfarers and the fortunate.
